strengths: Elegant and Unifying Framework: The paper successfully unifies a wide variety of existing preference optimization methods (including DPO, IPO, SPPO, INPO, REBEL, and DRO) under the mathematical lens of the Prox operator. This provides a highly cohesive perspective on the LLM alignment literature.

Robust Theoretical Guarantees: Last-iterate convergence is highly desirable in LLM alignment because iterate averaging is computationally impractical. COMAL is the first algorithm to provably achieve last-iterate convergence to an exact Nash equilibrium under general preferences. Importantly, the theoretical analysis covers both exact and approximate updates, making it highly relevant to practical deep learning settings.

Thorough and Rigorous Evaluation: The empirical evaluation is dual-pronged. A synthetic 3D cyclic game clearly illustrates the theoretical limitations of other methods (e.g., cycling in iterative DPO/IPO, bias in INPO) and how COMAL resolves them. Furthermore, the LLM fine-tuning of Qwen2-1.5B over 42 iterations shows excellent stability and win-rate improvements, demonstrating a much more thorough iterative training regime than prior works.

Excellent Clarity and Presentation: The paper is exceptionally well-written and structured. The background on game theory and proximal methods is clearly explained, and the transition from abstract optimization algorithms to practical LLM losses is seamless.
weaknesses: Clarification on Practical Hyperparameters: The connection between the theoretical Algorithm 1 (with $T$ outer iterations and $K$ inner iterations) and the actual training setup of the LLM experiments could be made more explicit. Page 12 mentions that the reference policy is updated at the beginning of the third training round (after 12 iterations). Explicitly detailing the exact mapping of training epochs, data splits, and reference policy updates in the context of $T$ and $K_t$ would improve reproducibility.

Evaluator Overlap: The evaluation of the LLM uses the same preference oracle (Llama-3-OffsetBias-8B) as the training data generation. While this is mathematically sound for validating the optimization of the specific game, testing the final models on an independent, stronger judge (e.g., GPT-4 or Claude) or standard benchmarks (e.g., AlpacaEval 2.0 LC) would further demonstrate if the optimization gains translate to general preference alignment without overfitting the training oracle.

strengths: Strong theoretical foundation: The paper applies the classical proximal point method (conceptual prox-method) to LLM alignment, proving last-iterate convergence to the exact Nash equilibrium of the unregularized game.

Addresses a key limitation: Unlike average-iterate convergence methods (which are computationally impractical for LLMs as they require averaging model outputs/parameters), COMAL provides a last-iterate guarantee.

Unifying perspective: Unifies multiple popular preference optimization algorithms (including PPO, DPO, IPO, SPPO, and INPO) as concrete implementations of the Prox operator, showing that COMAL acts as a versatile meta-algorithm.

Comprehensive evaluation: Validates the theory on both a controlled synthetic intransitive game (where the cycling/divergence of baselines is clearly visualized) and a practical LLM fine-tuning setup (Qwen2-1.5B on UltraFeedback).
weaknesses: Gap between theory and practice: Theoretically, the inner regularized game must be solved to high accuracy (with error $\epsilon_t \le O(1/t^4)$) at each outer iteration. In practice, due to compute limits, the authors use a heuristic update rule (updating the reference policy only once at the third training round). The implications of this gap on the last-iterate convergence guarantee should be discussed further.

Evaluation bias: The preference oracle used to generate the pairwise training data (Llama-3-OffsetBias-8B) is also used as the evaluator. Evaluating with an independent, stronger model (such as GPT-4) would make the experimental results more convincing and rule out oracle-exploitation bias.

Clarity of training terminologies: The mapping between the theoretical parameters (outer iteration $t$, inner iteration $k$) and the practical implementation details (training rounds, 6 data splits, 42 iterations) is somewhat confusing and could be clarified to improve readability.

strengths: Strong theoretical motivation: The paper addresses a key limitation in standard preference optimization—the reliance on the transitive Bradley-Terry assumption—by formulating alignment as a symmetric two-player zero-sum game under general preferences.

Provable last-iterate convergence: While prior work mostly guarantees average-iterate convergence (which is highly impractical for LLMs as iterate averaging is non-trivial), COMAL provably achieves last-iterate convergence to the exact Nash equilibrium policy.

Unifying perspective: The paper successfully frames several popular preference learning algorithms (DPO, IPO, SPPO, etc.) as implementations of the Prox operator, allowing them to be integrated into the proposed meta-algorithm as black-box subgame solvers.

Intuitive synthetic experiments: The 3D toy experiments effectively illustrate the cycling behavior of iterative DPO/IPO/SPPO and visually demonstrate how COMAL successfully converges to the Nash equilibrium.
weaknesses: Significant gap between theory and practice: According to Algorithms 1 and 4, the reference policy $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ must be updated at every outer iteration $t$. However, in the actual LLM experiments (Section 5.2), the reference policy was only updated once (at the beginning of the third training round, i.e., after 12 iterations out of 42). This heuristic deviation undermines the theoretical convergence guarantees. If updating at every iteration is too unstable or costly, the reasons should be thoroughly discussed, and the impact of this gap on the convergence proofs should be addressed.

Self-evaluation bias and lack of general benchmarks: The LLM experiments evaluate the models using the same preference oracle (Llama-3-OffsetBias-8B) that was used to generate the training data. This represents a closed-loop evaluation that risks severe overfitting to the specific evaluator's idiosyncrasies. To show true alignment capability, the authors should evaluate on standard external benchmarks like AlpacaEval (using GPT-4) or Arena-Hard.

Length bias exploitation: As shown in Figure 3 (right), the output length of COMAL increases rapidly during training, exceeding 2500 tokens. This suggests that the model might be winning primarily by exploiting the length bias of the Llama-3 preference oracle (a well-known issue where evaluators prefer longer responses). Including length-controlled win rates is highly recommended to verify if the alignment improvement is qualitative.

High computational complexity: Training for 42 iterations where each iteration takes 5 hours on 8 A6000 GPUs is extremely expensive for fine-tuning a 1.5B parameter model. This limits the practicality of the method compared to offline single-pass algorithms.

strengths: Strong game-theoretic and optimization-based foundation, modeling general LLM alignment as a two-player zero-sum game and addressing the critical issue of last-iterate convergence.

Excellent theoretical contributions, providing provable last-iterate convergence to the exact unregularized Nash equilibrium, even when the inner regularized games are solved only approximately (Theorem 3). This is much more practical than existing works requiring exact solutions.

A unified perspective that shows how many existing popular preference optimization algorithms (such as SPPO, DRO, REBEL, IPO, INPO) can be viewed as practical implementations of the prox operator, making COMAL a highly versatile meta-algorithm.

Solid empirical evaluation on both synthetic 3x3 games (which clearly illustrate the cycling behavior of baselines vs. the convergence of COMAL) and large-scale LLM alignment (Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B) using a non-transitive preference oracle mixture.
weaknesses: The multi-iteration nature of the algorithm (e.g., running 18 iterations/3 rounds on subsets of UltraFeedback) naturally increases the overall training complexity and scheduling overhead. While the authors state that the per-iteration computational cost is comparable, a clearer discussion on the trade-off between total training epochs/compute budget and the final win-rate gains would be beneficial.

The strategy for adjusting the KL-regularization strength across rounds (e.g., starting with $\eta^{-1} = 0.002$ and then adjusting to $0.1$ for subsequent rounds in Llama-3) is somewhat heuristic and may require careful tuning depending on the base model's initial alignment state.

The preference oracle used in the experiments is a mixture of two Bradley-Terry reward models. Although this mathematically induces intransitivity, it still represents a relatively structured non-BT setting. Evaluating on a highly non-transitive or human-annotated preference dataset with real-world noise would strengthen the empirical claims.

strengths: Strong and rigorous theoretical analysis: The paper establishes last-iterate convergence of the proposed meta-algorithm to the exact Nash equilibrium of the unregularized game. Crucially, Theorem 3 extends this result to the realistic case of approximate solvers, which is much more practical and robust than existing works.

Elegant unified perspective: The authors show that many existing algorithms (PPO, GRPO, DPO, IPO, SPPO, etc.) can be interpreted as implementations of the proximal operator. This enables COMAL to act as a versatile meta-algorithm that can be seamlessly integrated with existing training pipelines.

Well-designed and thorough evaluation: The authors validate COMAL on both a simple synthetic intransitive setup (proving the failure of existing methods) and on large-scale LLMs (Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B) using UltraFeedback. The results convincingly demonstrate that COMAL avoids training instability and maintains higher win rates compared to baselines.
Excellent writing and clarity: The paper is highly structured, and the progression from theoretical motivation to algorithmic design and empirical results is very smooth and easy to follow.
weaknesses: Increased computational cost: Since COMAL requires multiple outer loops (each running a sub-solver for several iterations), the overall training time is non-trivial. While the per-iteration cost is comparable, a more detailed discussion on the efficiency and trade-offs of the outer-loop budget (e.g., how to allocate inner vs. outer iterations under a fixed computational budget) would be helpful.

Hyperparameter sensitivity: The algorithm's stability and convergence depend on the careful tuning of regularization strengths (e.g., $\eta^{-1}$ and $\tau$). In the experiments, the authors had to dynamically adjust $\eta^{-1}$ from 0.002 to 0.1 to stabilize Llama-3 training. More systematic guidance on choosing these parameters would increase practical usability.

Simulated preference oracle: The LLM experiments rely on a simulated preference oracle (a mixture of two Bradley-Terry models) to generate intransitivity. While standard in the literature, it remains a simulated environment, and the performance under noisy, real-world human preferences remains to be fully explored.

strengths: Rigorous game-theoretic framework: The paper models general preference alignment as a symmetric two-player zero-sum game and successfully applies the proximal point algorithm (Conceptual Prox-method) to achieve last-iterate convergence to the unregularized Nash equilibrium.

Inexact convergence guarantees: Unlike previous theoretical works that assume exact Nash equilibrium solvers for the subproblems, this paper proves last-iterate convergence even when the regularized games are solved approximately (Theorem 3). This is highly realistic and practical for deep learning applications.

Modular meta-algorithmic design: COMAL is designed as a meta-algorithm that can seamlessly integrate various popular preference learning objectives (such as DPO, IPO, GRPO, SPPO, etc.) as the inner subproblem solver, requiring minimal changes to existing alignment pipelines.

Convincing experimental validation: The paper demonstrates the limitations of existing algorithms on a synthetic 3D cyclic game (showing that other algorithms cycle or suffer from a constant equilibrium gap) and provides large-scale experiments with competitive open-source models (Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B) on the UltraFeedback dataset, showing substantial win-rate improvements against strong baselines while preserving general performance on standard benchmarks.
weaknesses: High computational requirements: Iterative self-play algorithms are inherently expensive. Dividing the instruction set into multiple subsets and running up to 18 training iterations can be very computationally demanding (the authors note ~100 hours on 8x A6000 GPUs). A more explicit discussion or comparison on the computational trade-offs (e.g., total gradient steps/training time compared to single-round DPO/IPO) would strengthen the paper.

Complexity in hyperparameter scheduling: To achieve optimal results and avoid performance degradation under Llama-3, COMAL relies on a dynamic adjustment of the KL regularization strength (e.g., setting $\eta^{-1}$ to 0.002 for the first round and 0.1 for subsequent rounds). This adds heuristic complexity to the training pipeline compared to static-parameter algorithms.

Evaluation using the training preference oracle: While evaluating with the same preference oracle used during training provides a controlled environment to verify convergence, it might not fully reflect out-of-distribution human preferences. The results on standard benchmarks evaluated with GPT-4 (Table 3) show strong but more comparable results to the baselines.
